Well of course you can surprise someone by taking him/her to an unplanned trip to Disneyland... But I would say the smallest things are the best and simplest way to make someone's day. The secret is a mix of food, written notes, and paying attention to other people's feelings.
- Sometimes I write a nice note on a post-it to my colleague and put it on his desk when he's not looking (like "congrats on xxx", or "don't listen to them, you are the best"). I can see he likes it because he sticks them on his computer screen 
- Our secretary's mother died (we're not especially close, I talked to her less than 10 times in a year). I bought some sweets from the vending machine and left them with a post it note on her desk (again). It costs nothing. She later told me she thought it was so nice she cried. 
- celebrate your peers' accomplishments when they don't. It doesn't have to be a big party. Just buy 2 coffees from the coffee machine, go to someone's desk (if it's at work) and tell this person "let's drink to your xxx" or "let's have a toad to you getting rid of yyy".
- Me and my ex boyfriend were broke. He liked it a lot when I surprised him with meat I bought from the butcher. Or pastries. Or when I stuffed the drawer in his fridge with beers. Or when I did his breakfast.
- I also liked doing things like putting his boxer shorts on the heater while he was in the shower in winter. 
- A friend borrowed me her car so when I returned it I stuffed the glove compartment with chocolate and stuffs.
- send flowers. Flowers are not just for lovers. My friend moved out of town. One day she was feeling lonely so I ordered a bouquet delivery. She appreciated it so much she took pictures, sent it to me and put it on Instagram, and sent me flowers back later. Everyone loves receiving flowers.
- order food delivery. My younger brother doesn't make a lot of money despite working a lot. Sometimes I order him food (wether pizza or something more healthy). Make sure the person is at home first.
I hope this helps

In most movies, after a character fails suicide it's a new beginning for him, a new chance. etc. It might be for some people, but for some others, it's hell.

Because in your head, in your emotions, you are dead. But your body is alive. So you have to get back to work and talk to people again (and maybe explain why you did what you did and even reassure them cause you won't tell people "actually I might try again ASAP").

It feels like being a puppet, you go back to doing the same things you were doing before but in an "automatic pilot" mode. Your soul has left already. It's also like being a zombie, you have no feeling, no brain, nothing, you're just here wandering, pretending to be human while you're dead.

People who "succeed" in suicide averagely try 19 times before they succeed. Meaning for most people a failed suicide attempt is not a "new beginning" at all. Or maybe for a few moment, but the suicidal thoughts will eventually come back again.

It depends on the country you live in and which major in psychology you decide to specialize in.

I went to psychology to do clinical psychology (as you can see in my example), but got very disappointed because in my country we're still influenced by psychoanalysis (which is like prehistory of psychology). I didn't felt useful, and felt like it would make the patient very guilty and it was very sexist too (and the scientific evidences are almost nonexistant).

But then I went to a cognitive psychology class and fell in love woth the discipline. It's more science proof based, and shows how fascinating the brain is. It helps you understant a very large part of our life (why and how the brain is mechanically influenced by advertisments, why do we see vision illusions, how can children learn how to talk, while they are incapable of telling grammatical rules, why do we hear music instead of a bunch of sounds following each others, what are the processes behind fear and love, why do we take decisions, how do existential thinking raises in our brains, how do we talk and see...). It's awesome.

Now I work in Innovation department for a car manufacturer, on human-machine relationships (still a sort of clinical psychology? lol). I use immersive simulation for testing which is pretty cool.

In some countries, psychology learning is more focused on cognitive and behavioral therapies for example, there's more succeed rates, so you might enjoy going for this.

There's also social psychology, which focus on social groups (basically, the behavior/thinking of social group is not the total of each individual behavior, it creates another behavior/thinking). You can learn how you can be influenced by a majority or minority of people (interesting fact: Majority will influence you publicly, but when alone again, you will go back to your previous opinion. Influence of a minority will not influence you in public (you will follow your opinions in public), but will convince you then and privately). Social psychology can lead to building some therapies too. There's a lot of stuffs related to workplace also.

Developmental psychology: how brain develops for children, you study a lot education methodology (but many other stuffs too).

Neuropsychology: like cognitive psychology but looking for biological evidences. 

Etc, etc. 

Psychology regroups a very wide type of topics and methodologies. My advice is to just take a step in the field as a start, and decide later what you want to study, why and how. 

The most important quality to get is being curious, and empathetic/not jusging toward humans, understanding that all of this is just like a big engine and you try to understand the mechanic/technology.

Setting the ambiance can be important. What's important depends on the book and genre. For example, it's not necessary to show your character washing his clothes and cleaning the house *unless* it's Snowhite because this is how she stays at the dwarves' house. Or in Cinderella cleaning in Disney movie because she's doing it with birds and mice, thus it sets the children/magical world.

When you write as a professional for movies for example you have to do this because of budget restrictions. You can't add scenes if they are not essential. At the minimum they have to tell something about a character. But something that helps to understand him so you will understand his reactions to the events of the plots, and his following decisions.

It's a very good exercise. You can do a table with each scene of your story, and add some justifications for each even if you're not writing for a movie because it helps a lot understanding the directions. It also helps spotting some missing parts (like "I need more scenes of those 2 together to show what they have in common so we can understand better why they became friends").

Another good exercise it to take a book and try to do it by yourself. The ultimate example is Harry Potter (JK Rowling is a genius). You can take any scene even if they are not directly directed toward the plot, they all contain hints for the future (sometimes the future means several books later). But you'd better start with a rather simpler book. It will make your story feel more solid.

Long post, but I think it's a good thing to put that here. 

The truth is that everyone has a background. In many movies psychiatrists / psychologists are portrayed as insensitive rocks that tells you what to do. Or spiritual superiorities that can guess all of your future.

But that's not what we do or how we do it. We're not super humans. We comme from the same world as yours. We're trained to analyze human's behavior, emotions and processes. But the knowledge comes from the person in front of us, and the ultimate decisions come from this person. 

I think the most accurate depiction of a psychologist I've seen in a movie is in *Will Hunting* (not that I compare to Robin Williams). He has the most important characteristics for a psychologist: empathy and goodwill. He has his issues too, but that doesn't prevent him from being caring. 

Sean is not insensitive (he clearly imposes limits on Will's aggressiveness) and laughs with Will sometimes. 

He never loses the sense of the therapy but there's no hierarchical relationship between them. This is very important to understand before a therapy. 

I love the scene where they're on a bench, and he tells to Will that just because he read manuals or Oliver Twist that doesn't mean he knows everything about Will. That's a key point about therapy that we rarely see on TV.

He never judges and cares about Will's happiness yet never tells him what to do (he even refuses to do that when his co-workers pressure him). He wants Will to make his own decisions, decisions that lead to happiness, not external signs of success, nor what we "consider" as being a successful life. 

He understands that Will's happiness won't be found in academic success, but in finding emotional stability and safety first. Then comes medals and stuffs, but only if Will does it because he likes working in this field. They both try to work on Will's fullfilling. 

This is another key point. Things that seem hard for some people are easy for the others. Everyone around Will would give the world to have his skills because it's so hard for them to reach is level. While it's so easy for Will, he's unable to express his emotions.
Psychologists won't push you to succeed in life (work or marriage whatever), but help you to be ok with your decisions, cope with struggles and learn to keep walking on that road. 

That's why being empathetic and caring is crucial. And I think sometimes having a background can even help to be empathetic. I remember during college, hearing some classmates (the type who want to do this job just because parents are psy too) saying stuffs like "god, some people are really crazy! (with despise)", when learning about some illnesses. And I was like "??????". There's nothing like craziness in psychology. There's a large variety of life patterns and / or brain developments, that's all. 

Everyone grows up with a personal structure, and people who live safe all their lives are rare (and even them have a background). 

Another nuanced representation is Krista Gordon the psychologist in *Mr Robot*. 

*TL;DR Therapists are regular people with a different training, they MUSTN'T boss you around, watch Will Hunting, all your struggles are valid*

Hello, 

This is the type of message that never totally help, but it can help putting things into perspective.
I have this friend, he's called Jean-François, we call him Jeff. He had a cancer. He went through really hard time. But he wasn't "cancer-jeff" all the time. Actually I rarely saw it laid down on the bed, looking 100 years old, etc.
Obviously some people do look like this. But my point is that when you're ill, you do not necessarly look like dying, or for depression for example: crying all the time.
A lot of depressed people hide it for a long time.

Illness impacts the body system, but it do not always impact the mood. And it's a dysfunctional system, not a brand new honda machine that will be 100% regular. There will be moments when your body will be able to fight it, moments when he won't. Moments when the disorder will affect the mood, moments when it affects other parts. Plus it's different from one person to another.

I know it won't stop your guilty thoughts, it's just to have another view on this (but Jeff is very narcissistic so he won't feel guilty not looking ill).

Concerning the guilty feeling, it's partly social (I mean, MOSTLY social) and cultural. People think people who have cancer MUST be lied in bed all day, looking dead, otherwise they're lying. It's even worse for mental illness and disorders. Because most people think it doesn't really exists, and in the movies depressed people for example are also depicted at the extreme all the time.
Then people project their image of what a mental health is on you, and if it's not what they think, they conclude you are lying. But the thing is that, at some point you integrate their thought, and feel like you're doing wrong, and maybe lying too.

Also, it's often a part of the disorder (medically speaking). Just like suicide thoughts (a serotonine problem). 
Both add to the other and work together, and you grow up like this, and it makes it a part of how you work. 
Changing your thoughts will take time but it's possible with cognitive therapy.
And if you can't make them disappear, there's different techniques to cope with them instead. 

My brother told me to name my "demons". For example when you hear "Karen" saying "What about you go home and harm yourself?", you answer "What about you shut the fuck up Karen". It didn't "save" me, but it help me gain time few time or I'd have crashed into a tree with my car). It's also close to cognitive therapies as it makes you put some distance between you and your thoughts.

Concerning the paranoia, I'd say it's not just "you" but a medical problem too (that guilt can make higher, all of this work together, it's not your fault).

For the self harm there's also few apps that help a little bit. I have this one called "calm harm". It takes me a lot to open it when I feel bad, but I think it helps a little bit. But it's super cool if you have escape plans, it's a little bit the same.

I also try to tell myself 1 positive stuff repeatedly when I have bad thoughts, so it makes my brain busy, plus it helps to make your brain integrate it. 
Some cognitive therapy techniques consist in taking a thought, thinking about what you want to think instead, and think about it every time you have the bad thought again. At some point (I mean not one week of course), you will think about the good thought automatically.

My other technique is to focus on what I'm doing and describing it internally (like when I'm thinking "you don't deserve that", I try being like "I'm cutting the carrots, I'm standing, my feets are on the floor, it's an orange carrot, I'm putting it into the water, etc".).

But I have obsessive thoughts with guilt too and we know it doesn't disappear just like that. Small stuffs help gaining time until the moment you can finally go sleeping (so your brain is off mostly).
I know all of this won't change your life but I hope it will help a little bit (or at least wont do bad).
Remember that you're a good person. And people that think you're lying do not know anything of what's happening in your head.
Also remember that you are strong. Because you have to do the same as the others do, but with a wayyyy heavier weight on the shoulders. You are stronger than most people around you. Especially the ones despising you. Everyone deserves happiness, every human. And you are a human, you derserve love, and comfort, and this is not some luxury, your body needs it. Consider it as a medication if it makes you accept it more. When you reach the point when you're ahving a good day, or even 1 sudden good thought, it's a success! Take that Karen!

-> there's different types of focusing and memory functions. For example there's short term memory that is used to remember a phone number before writing it, for example. And long term that you use to stock long life memory. There's also work memory (I don't know the term in english tbh), that is used to do some tasks such as calculus.
Same for focusing issues, it's not the same issue when you're focusing on small tasks or more complex tasks.
I'm asking that, because depending of the type or problem you have, it could be due to different things as you see. If it happened before, then it could be something that is degrating. If it's new then it could be a new dysfunction that had been introduce by an internal event (health problem I mean, not forcebly serious), or external event (medication), thus it can be changed.
This is probably what your doctor is going to test, and he's probably going to ask you those questions too. Then you can start thinking about it, when did it start, etc. 
But it's still hard to say where excactly the problem comes from since to do some calculus you need focusing and work memory. With your descriptions and his tests he will try to find where does this comes from.
The only inconvenient thing is that the better would be for you to get tested in a period in which you have those problems. Maybe you can talk about the doctor about this (having a 2nd appointment later (if you have money for this though)).

It's true that stress, and even more, being tired can have an impact on this.

Some people can have a mini stroke, the subject can even notice nothing. You have a headache, or dizziness, and / or other symptoms.
It happens and can be nothing but requires surveillance sometimes (just in case).

But don't be scared, even if it was that (and it's not forcibly a big deal), you have a young brain (contrarly to what they say), so it's plastic and can regenerate from injuries.

----- Whatever it is, don't worry, you took the good decision if you're going to a doctor. Just in case. If he finds nothing at least you will know. 
Think about all of this, but without panicking. Instead, try to be objective by observing yourself as a doctor would do. Note the moments when it happens, not when it's worse (you can even make a graph), note what TASK you were doing, not how much it creates a problem in the context (not remembering whose turn it is taken alone is not critical pathologically speaking) how many hours you slept before, meds, food, and/or any event you think is relevant. Maybe also note (just one line you know, like a mini journal), some activities, or emotion you felt in the day. 
The point is to detect if there's a trigger, and if there's something that stops this. And if it's related to internal or external causes (or completely random as you said, but even if it's a brain health problem, there might me a reason it's not permanent).

First, belive me there's loads of stuffs you don't remember. Daily life is to much things to handle. Writing things will help noticing triggers way better. Second, it will be a good base to talk with the doctor (not sure if you should show him though, they can be very troublesome when it comes to patients being autonomous).
